qs.q: An infant is diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot, characterized by pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. A single developmental error explains this constellation; what is it?
o: Primary agenesis of the superior endocardial cushion
Unequal asymmetric division of the truncus arteriosus
Failure of the septum secundum to cover the foramen
Complete absence of the embryonic sinus venosus horn
Premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus vessel
qs.e: Unequal division of the truncus arteriosus by the aortopulmonary septum causes both pulmonary stenosis and the VSD.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Embryology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four cardinal features of Tetralogy of Fallot?
o: Left atrial dilation
Ventricular septal defect
Overriding aorta
Right ventricular hypertrophy
qs.e: The four cardinal features of Tetralogy of Fallot are overriding aorta, ventricular septal defect, right ventricular hypertrophy, and subpulmonic stenosis. Left atrial dilation is not a primary component of this anomaly.

qs.q: Which of the following structural abnormalities is a core component of Tetralogy of Fallot?
o: Presence of atrial septal defect
Presence of right ventricular hypertrophy
Presence of left ventricular hypertrophy
Presence of bicuspid aortic valve
qs.e: Tetralogy of Fallot consists of a VSD, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Left ventricular hypertrophy is not part of this tetrad.

qs.q: A 2-month-old infant with Tetralogy of Fallot is brought for evaluation. Which type of cardiac murmur is most characteristic of this condition?
o: High-pitched decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
Pansystolic murmur radiating widely across the precordium
Continuous machinery murmur audible throughout the cardiac cycle
Ejection systolic murmur heard best at the upper left sternal border
qs.e: The characteristic murmur of Tetralogy of Fallot is an ejection systolic murmur caused by turbulent flow across the right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. A pansystolic murmur is more typical of an isolated ventricular septal defect.

qs.q: A chest radiograph is obtained for an infant presenting with intermittent cyanosis and hypercyanotic spells. Which radiographic finding is classic for Tetralogy of Fallot?
o: Prominent left atrial and ventricular enlargement
Boot-shaped heart with an upturned apex
Global cardiomegaly with increased vascularity
Narrow mediastinum with a snowman appearance
qs.e: Right ventricular hypertrophy and an upturned apex give the heart a boot-shaped (coeur en sabot) appearance on chest radiography in Tetralogy of Fallot. Global cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary blood flow is typical of large left-to-right shunts rather than TOF.

qs.q: Which of the following interventions has no role in the acute management of a hypercyanotic spell (tet spell) in Tetralogy of Fallot?
o: Intravenous morphine sulfate for analgesia
Administration of sodium bicarbonate intravenously
Use of phenobarbitone as a sedative
Intravenous propranolol to reduce heart rate
qs.e: Phenobarbitone has no role in the management of tet spells, while sodium bicarbonate, morphine, propranolol, and knee-chest positioning are standard supportive or medical treatments. The wrong option is plausible as a sedative, but unlike morphine, it does not alleviate infundibular spasm.

qs.q: The fundamental embryological defect in Tetralogy of Fallot is
o: Failure of the truncus to divide properly
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
Absence of the tricuspid valve leaflets
Anterior and superior displacement of the infundibular septum
qs.e: The 'monology' of Fallot is the anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum, which leads to VSD, subpulmonary stenosis, and overriding aorta.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - March 7, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: In Tetralogy of Fallot, which level is the dominant site of right ventricular outflow obstruction?
o: Valvular
Supravalvular
Subvalvular (infundibular)
At the pulmonary bifurcation
qs.e: The dominant obstruction in TOF is at the subvalvular/infundibular level due to hypertrophied infundibular myocardium from the malaligned outlet septum — not at the valve itself.

es.q: Outline the features and non-role management of Tetralogy of Fallot based on the provided text.
es.m:
- **Presenting features:** Includes right ventricular outflow obstruction, right ventricular hypertrophy, an overriding aorta, and a ventricular septal defect.
- **Additional features:** Aortic stenosis is noted as an incorrect feature.
- **Ineffective management interventions:** Phenobarbitone has no role in the management of Tetralogy of Fallot.
- **Effective management interventions:** Sodium bicarbonate, morphine, propranolol, and knee-chest positioning are utilized.

es.q: **Boot-shaped heart and Tet spells?** **Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)**.
es.m:
- **Pathology:** The most common cyanotic congenital heart disease characterised by four classic anatomical components.
- **Components:** Ventricular septal defect (VSD), pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH).
- **Tet spells:** Episodes of sudden, severe cyanosis and hyperpnoea, often triggered by crying or feeding.
- **Compensatory posture:** Children instinctively squat during spells to increase systemic vascular resistance, which reduces right-to-left shunting and improves pulmonary blood flow.
- **Radiological sign:** Chest X-ray classically demonstrates a 'boot-shaped heart' (*coeur en sabot*) due to right ventricular hypertrophy.

es.q: **Boot-shaped heart and Tet spells?** Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF).
es.m:
- **Pathology**: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease, characterised by four cardinal features: VSD, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH).
- **Tet Spells**: Characterized by sudden episodes of profound cyanosis and hyperpnea, often triggered by crying, feeding, or agitation.
- **Mechanism of Relief**: Squatting relieves these spells by increasing systemic vascular resistance, which reduces right-to-left shunting and improves pulmonary blood flow.
- **Radiological Findings**: Chest X-ray classically demonstrates a 'boot-shaped heart' (*coeur en sabot*) due to right ventricular hypertrophy and an upturned apex.

ai.title: Tetralogy of Fallot
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic congenital heart defect with a ventricular septal defect, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy. It presents with cyanotic spells, a harsh systolic ejection murmur and clubbing. Management centres on surgical repair, with supportive care for hypoxaemia.

sections.p: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is a combination of four cardiac anomalies that cause right‑to‑left shunting and cyanosis. Diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by echocardiography. In low‑resource settings, a focused bedside echo or a portable handheld device can suffice.
b: Cyanosis, especially during crying or exertion
Harsh systolic ejection murmur at left upper sternal border
Digital clubbing
Tet spells (paroxysmal cyanosis relieved by squatting)

t.b: Shows VSD, pulmonary infundibular stenosis, overriding aorta, RV hypertrophy – confirms TOF
SpO2 <90% on room air, improves with squatting or handgrip
Boot‑shaped heart, prominent pulmonary arteries – supportive but not diagnostic

sections.p: Severity is graded by the degree of pulmonary stenosis and cyanosis. The most widely used system is the Ross classification: Stage I (mild), II (moderate), III (severe).
b: Stage I – mild infundibular stenosis, SpO2 90–95%
Stage II – moderate, SpO2 80–90%
Stage III – severe, SpO2 <80% or frequent spells

sections.p: TOF is a sporadic developmental defect of the outflow tract. In low‑resource settings, maternal infections (rubella, HIV), malnutrition, and teratogenic exposures (alcohol, certain herbal remedies) are considered risk factors.
b: Genetic mutations (e.g., NKX2‑5, NOTCH1) – rare
Maternal rubella infection – uncommon in vaccinated populations
Maternal HIV – possible immunological effect
Malnutrition – zinc or folate deficiency

sections.p: Classic presentation is a young child with cyanosis, especially during crying or exertion, a harsh systolic murmur, and clubbing. Tet spells are episodic cyanosis relieved by squatting.
b: Cyanosis at rest or with activity
Harsh systolic ejection murmur
Digital clubbing
Tet spells – sudden cyanosis, pallor, tachycardia

sections.p: Investigation priorities are rapid, bedside‑friendly tests. When advanced imaging is unavailable, clinical assessment and basic labs guide management.

t.b: Normal heart size and pulmonary vasculature

sections.p: Urgent red flags include severe hypoxaemia, heart failure, arrhythmias, and infection. Complications can be acute (tet spells, heart failure) or chronic (pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmia).
b: SpO2 <70% or worsening despite squatting
Rapidly increasing cyanosis
Signs of heart failure – tachypnoea, hepatomegaly

sections.p: Management is staged: initial stabilization, then definitive surgical repair. Supportive care focuses on oxygenation, fluid balance and infection prevention.
b: Oxygen therapy – 2–4 L/min via nasal cannula or face mask

t.b: Avoid if ductus is already closed

sections.p: Post‑repair follow‑up includes monitoring for residual shunt, arrhythmia and pulmonary hypertension. Prevention focuses on maternal health and vaccination.
b: Regular ECG and echo at 6 months, 1 year, then annually

sections.p: Conditions that mimic TOF include other cyanotic CHDs (e.g., transposition of the great arteries), severe asthma, and severe anemia.
b: Transposition of the great arteries – harsh systolic murmur, cyanosis but no pulmonary stenosis

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, a normal chest X‑ray can miss TOF; a normal SpO2 on rest may be misleading if the child is not exerted.
b: SpO2 may be >90% at rest but drop during activity

t.b: An episode of sudden cyanosis, pallor and tachycardia, relieved by squatting or handgrip.
Increases systemic vascular resistance, reducing right‑to‑left shunt and improving oxygenation.
All patients with moderate to severe TOF; early repair reduces mortality and improves growth.

faq.a: An acute cyanotic episode relieved by squatting or handgrip.
It increases systemic vascular resistance, reducing the right‑to‑left shunt.
All patients with moderate to severe TOF; early repair improves outcomes.

exam: What is the most likely cause of a 2‑year‑old with cyanosis, a harsh systolic murmur and clubbing? — VSD with pulmonary stenosis (Tetralogy of Fallot).
During a tet spell, which manoeuvre is most effective? — Squatting or handgrip to increase SVR.
A child with TOF presents with SpO2 78% on room air. What is the next step? — Start oxygen therapy and arrange urgent echo.
What is the key echocardiographic finding in TOF? — VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary infundibular stenosis and RV hypertrophy.
Why is prostaglandin E1 used in severe TOF? — To keep the ductus arteriosus open and maintain systemic flow.
Which complication is most common after TOF repair? — Pulmonary regurgitation leading to RV dilation.
